cards.text: The National Park Service says the Buckstaff Bathhouse opened on February 1, 1912, and has been in continuous operation since.
Eight historic bathhouses stand on Hot Springs' Bathhouse Row: Superior, Hale, Maurice, Fordyce, Quapaw, Ozark, Buckstaff and Lamar.
The Hale, built in 1892-93, is the oldest surviving bathhouse on Bathhouse Row, according to the Encyclopedia of Arkansas.
The Maurice Bathhouse added a therapeutic pool in 1931 to treat paralysis, and it was the only bathhouse to employ a registered physical therapist.
The Hale Bathhouse once had a sweat cave in the tufa bluff called the "electric cave", which closed in 1911.
Hot Springs' Running of the Tubs bathtub race began in 2006, and racers push their tubs the length of Bathhouse Row.
cards.source: Visit Hot Springs: Running of the Tubs 2026 press release

cards.text: Hot Springs declared a city holiday for Oaklawn's first day of racing, and more than 3,000 people attended, according to Wikipedia.
Zachary Taylor Davis designed Oaklawn's original 1904 clubhouse, and he later designed Wrigley Field and Old Comiskey Park.
Former President Theodore Roosevelt attended the 1910 Arkansas State Fair in Oaklawn's infield, which the state fair used from 1906 to 1914.
Oaklawn's meet, held December through May, is sometimes called the "Fifth Season," according to Wikipedia.
Smarty Jones collected Oaklawn's $5 million centennial bonus in 2004 for sweeping its three-year-old graded stakes and winning the Kentucky Derby.
The Hot Springs Mountain Tower is a lattice steel tower 216 feet tall, opened to the public on June 3, 1983.
The steel Rix Tower, which opened in 1906 and had an elevator for visitors, preceded today's Hot Springs Mountain Tower.
Hot Springs' thermal spring water averages about 143°F, and the National Park Service calls the springs the hottest east of the Rocky Mountains.
The National Park Service says the Hot Springs thermal springs produce over 700,000 gallons of water a day.
The USGS found that most Hot Springs thermal water is about 4,400 years old, with a very small share under 20 years old.
The USGS says Hot Springs National Park is best known for its 47 hot springs, which emerge from Hot Springs Mountain.
In 1886 the Chicago White Stockings became the first major league club to hold spring training in Hot Springs.
The Historic Baseball Trail says Babe Ruth trained in Hot Springs nine times and became a very familiar face around town.
cards.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

cards.text: Wikipedia says more than 130 Hall of Famers played or trained at Hot Springs' Whittington/Ban Johnson Park, including Ruth, Cy Young and Ty Cobb.
Hot Springs' George Barr school, which ran from 1935 to 1947, is recognized as the first umpire school in baseball.
Babe Didrikson attended Hot Springs' Ray Doan baseball school in 1934, where the instructors included Rogers Hornsby and Bob Feller.
Hot Springs native James Rector was the first Olympian from Arkansas, and he won an Olympic silver medal.
Future home-run king Hank Aaron, then 18, played a Negro League World Series game in Hot Springs on Oct. 1, 1952, with the Indianapolis Clowns.
cards.source: Hot Springs Historic Baseball Trail: See the Trail

cards.text: Hot Springs High alumnus Antwon Hicks, class of 2000, is a 2016 Olympian and 2002 World Junior Championships gold medalist.
